newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy graft probe plunges murky arms trade world.
newsitem.headline: Italy graft probe plunges murky arms trade world.

text.p: A huge graft scandal that has shocked corruption-weary Italians took a dramatic new turn on Sunday with revelations that state companies might have sent illegal arms shipments to Bosnia and Iraq.

The investigations detonated a week ago following the arrest of the head of the national railways and have quickly snowballed to reveal a "superlobby" of businessmen, judges and lawyers operating across a swathe of state sectors.
A new wave of police raids at company and legal offices in Milan, Rome and Turin were ordered by prosecutors on Saturday.

Commentators said this latest scandal could prove more devastating than the original "Tangentopoli" (Bribesville) probes in the early 1990s which swept away the country's post-war political establishment.

The new twist in the case came with the publication in newspapers of transcripts of tapped telephone conversations between state-owned arms firm Oto Melara and banker Pierfrancesco Pacini Battaglia, linchpin of the probe.
Reference is made in the phone calls to exports to Bosnia at a time when civil war in the former Yugoslavia was still raging and arms sales were banned by the United Nations.
Newspapers said the transcripts also pointed to the sale of heavy guns to the Iraqi navy as well as "vast arms traffic" moved with the help of the Sicilian Mafia.
Both Pacini Battaglia, who appeared to exert influence in a number of state companies, and the managing director of Oto Melara, Pierfrancesco Guarguaglini, are under arrest.

Magistrates in the tiny northwest port town of La Spezia, who are leading the investigations, have asked the defence ministry and foreign trade ministry to hand over documents concerning the Italian arms business.

The scandal, which has dominated the news in Italy for the past week, has dealt a serious blow to the country's image at a time when a political solution to the original Tangentopoli probes appeared to be within reach.

"By now it is clear that a small magistrates office in La Spezia has got in its hands on the heart of the Second Republic," Ezio Mauro, editor of left-leaning La Repubblica newspaper, said in a front page article.

The probe began when two young magistrates in La Spezia started to investigate alleged illegal car imports into Italy on the state railways, but has rapidly expanded to touch on key state concerns following a hi-tech surveillance operation.

Phone taps and secret video cameras appear to reveal a far- reaching network of trial fixing and bribes paid in return for lucrative state contracts. Some 50 hours-worth of phone conversations have still to be monitored.
"From what one reads in the press, it seems the magistrates have put their hands on something which is really huge," deputy prime minister Walter Veltroni told reporters on Sunday.

A junior La Spezia prosecutor sent a shiver through parliament and the financial markets last week when he said politicians were caught up in the affiar but his boss, Antonio Conte, swiftly denied this.

Luciano Violante, the speaker of the lower house of parliament, was quoted as saying in Sunday's newspapers that politicians, who took hefty bribes in Tangentopoli, were being by-passed by corrupt officials in the enormous state sector.

"These people now have the reins of power in their hands while the politicians are either busy doing other things or else are fools who don't understand what is going on, or else are not capable of tackling such a dangerous phenomenon," he said.
